slides.eyebrow: Never, ever skip this on an older NJ home
slides.sub: After 6 years in NJ real estate, these are the 3 checks I'd make before an older home is mine.

slides.title: Older homes, hidden tanks
slides.body: Older NJ homes may have a heating oil tank, and some tanks are buried underground. Old tanks can rust and leak. If one leaks, the tank owner must hire a certified pro to clean it up.
slides.source: NJDEP, Heating Oil Tanks; UHOT Homeowner's Guide (Oct. 2026)

slides.title: Ask the seller in writing
slides.body: Ask if there's an oil tank now, or if one was removed. Ask for the paperwork. If a tank ever leaked, ask for the NJDEP No Further Action letter.

slides.title: Ask your inspector to check
slides.body: NJ urges homeowners with oil tanks to have them tested and inspected. Ask your home inspector how to check for a buried tank, inside your inspection window, so you have time to act.

slides.title: Found one? Sort it out before closing
slides.body: NJDEP says a tank with no sign of a leak doesn't have to be removed. It's not uncommon for real estate pros to recommend removal before a sale. Talk to a real estate attorney about your situation.

caption:
Never, ever skip the oil tank check on an older NJ home. A buried tank you didn't know about can turn into your cleanup.

Older NJ homes may have a heating oil tank, and some are buried underground. Old tanks can rust and leak. If one leaks, the tank owner has to hire a certified pro to clean it up. Ask the seller in writing about any tank, current or removed, and ask for the paperwork. If a tank ever leaked, ask for the NJDEP No Further Action letter. Ask your home inspector how to check for a buried tank, inside your inspection window. NJDEP doesn't require removing a tank with no sign of a leak, but it's not uncommon for real estate pros to recommend removal before a sale.

Talk to a real estate attorney about your situation.
